title: Consistency models
summary: Compare linearizability, sequential consistency, causal consistency, eventual consistency, and four client-centric guarantees from Lecture 3, then connect them to MongoDB and ScyllaDB design choices.
objectives: Distinguish what linearizability, sequential consistency, causal consistency, and eventual consistency each promise
Explain the difference between read-your-writes, writes-follow-reads, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes
Relate read or write concerns, Lamport-clock session tracking, and digest read repair to concrete database behavior

sourceRefs.role: MongoDB read-your-writes implementation with Lamport clocks

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture 3 is where Atlas must keep four different boundaries straight: real-time order, causal order, eventual convergence, and one client's own session guarantees. The common failure mode is treating a weaker model as if it implied a stronger one.

sections.title: Data-centric guarantees
sections.body: Linearizability preserves real-time order and the most recent write, sequential consistency keeps one common order without the same real-time constraint, causal consistency preserves only causally related writes, and eventual consistency promises convergence only after updates stop.

sections.title: Client-centric guarantees and deployed systems
sections.body: Read-your-writes, writes-follow-reads, monotonic reads, and monotonic writes describe what one client can safely observe across replicas. MongoDB and ScyllaDB expose these trade-offs through read/write concerns, coordinator logic, Lamport-clock session state, digest reads, and read repair.

sourceRefs.role: MongoDB read-your-writes implementation with Lamport clocks

examples.title: Diagnose a stale-read path
steps: Classify the failure first: real-time order, causal dependency, eventual convergence, or one client's session view.
If the system uses MongoDB majority read/write concerns, ask whether the client still needs session or Lamport-clock state to preserve read-your-writes.
If the system uses tunable consistency, state the replication factor, chosen consistency level, and what stale or divergent read the coordinator may still permit.
Choose the weakest guarantee that rules out the observed anomaly instead of jumping immediately to the strongest global model.
examples.answer: A useful consistency diagnosis names the violated observation, the minimal guarantee that would prevent it, and the implementation mechanism that must carry that guarantee into the running database.

sourceRefs.role: MongoDB read-your-writes implementation with Lamport clocks

examples.title: History classifier and digest repair
steps: Draw the causal chain $W(x{=}1) \to W(y{=}2)$ before judging what another process reads.
If the observer sees $y{=}2$ and then $x{=}0$, the effect appeared without its cause, so causal consistency is violated.
For a separate replica read, compare compact digests first; a mismatch means the coordinator must fetch full versions.
Reconcile the full values, return the newest version, and repair stale replicas so future reads converge faster.
examples.answer: Consistency diagnosis has two distinct traces: preserve causal order in a history, then follow the digest-mismatch branch through full read, reconciliation, and repair.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which model additionally preserves real-time order between non-overlapping operations?
contrastDrills.explanation: Linearizability keeps the real-time order of non-overlapping operations; sequential consistency keeps one legal sequence but does not require the same real-time alignment.
contrastDrills.misconception: One common order is not automatically the same as preserving wall-clock non-overlap.

contrastDrills.prompt: A client writes $x=7$ and later reads $x$. Which client-centric guarantee is the minimum requirement to ensure that client sees the write?
contrastDrills.explanation: Read-your-writes guarantees that the same client sees its own completed write. Monotonic reads only prevents that client from moving backward after a prior read.
contrastDrills.misconception: Monotonic reads compares two reads; it does not by itself guarantee visibility of the client's own write.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which operation usually requires records to move between partitions?
contrastDrills.explanation: Grouping by key brings records with the same key together and typically requires a shuffle.
contrastDrills.misconception: Roadmap topics still need a stated system boundary before they become measured claims.

contrastDrills.prompt: What should Atlas show when the overview names a later topic but its detailed lecture is not supplied?
choices: Label it as a roadmap/context pointer
Copy a generic answer without a source
contrastDrills.explanation: Keep the roadmap pointer visible and mark detailed coverage pending until the appropriate lecture or official source is available.
contrastDrills.misconception: A roadmap mention is not the same thing as a source-backed derivation.

math.name: Linearizability real-time constraint
math.purpose: Use it to separate linearizability from weaker models that keep a legal sequence but not the same real-time ordering between non-overlapping operations.
math.explanation: If operation $op_1$ finishes before $op_2$ begins, a linearizable history must place $op_1$ before $op_2$ in the global sequence.

symbols.meaning: order in the legal global sequence

math.name: Causal-write visibility constraint
math.purpose: Use it to express that causally related writes must be observed in the same order, while concurrent writes may still be seen differently under weaker models.
math.explanation: If write $w_1$ causally precedes write $w_2$, any process $p$ that observes both must not observe $w_2$ before $w_1$.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why are MongoDB read concern "majority" and write concern "majority" still not sufficient by themselves to guarantee read-your-writes consistency by definition?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate majority-committed visibility from one client's session-level guarantee.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A majority-committed snapshot can still lag the client's latest write on the node that serves the read. MongoDB therefore needs additional session or Lamport-clock state to block until the serving node has caught up to that client's write.

sourceRefs.role: MongoDB read-your-writes implementation with Lamport clocks

criticalQuestions.prompt: When is a total global order stronger than the application actually needs?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare a workload that only cares about one client or one causal dependency with a workload that truly needs one identical order for every process.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: If the application only needs the same client to see its own writes or only needs causally related updates preserved, forcing one total order can add latency and coordination cost without buying a required guarantee.
